column11: Might increase it by benefiting existing renters and hurting new renters.

column5: We have tried this kind of policy many times and it will benefit some people who get locked in below market rates, but raise costs for others who need to rent apartments that are not capped and supply will fall.
column8: The literature review cited below was sponsored by a self-interested party, but in this case the facts are pretty clear.  Economists have shown over and over, if you cap prices you will reduce the supply available to buy.
column11: Some of the winners whose rents get capped will be wealthy people.  This too blunt an instrument (i.e. not targeted to helped lower income people) to deliver this kind of payoff.

column5: The cap might make people who already have rented an apartment better off, but will make it harder for those who haven't to find one.
column8: The rent cap gives landlords an incentive to withdraw housing units from the rental market and also blunts the incentive to build new units.
column11: The argument here is the same as for issue 1: some lower-income people will be helped; others will be hurt. I'm not sure what the overall effect on income inequality will be.

column5: Experience indicates that rent caps or controls typically backfire.  Even without adverse side effects, the policy is too meager to have a substantial effect.
